newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government says on course on deficit cuts.
newsitem.headline: French government says on course on deficit cuts.

text.p: The French government, rebuffing speculation France may face a big deficit overshoot in 1997, said on Thursday the trend so far this year showed it was on course to meet Maastricht Treaty criteria.
"I stick to my target. France will qualify for the euro," Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure said in a televised debate.

The opposition Socialist party, campaigning ahead of a two-round parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1, has called for an audit of public finances if it wins power to see how near France is to meeting Maastricht criteria.

It says it will not impose further austerity just to reduce the deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, but will instead seek negotiations with Germany and France's other European partners on a flexible interpretation of the Treaty.
Its call for a public audit has fueled speculation of a big gap in France's public finances this year which could require the new government to impose new spending cuts.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis however, told a news conference that budget trends so far had been satisfying.
Provisional data for April confirmed the trend shown in March which showed the central government budget deficit at 121.7 billion francs, 21.4 billion less than at the same time a year earlier.
Lamassoure said latest figures showed the deficit was 10 billion lower in April, although an official said this was based on early data for the month. Final figures were not yet known.
Lamassoure, who is also government spokesman, said that talk of a big gap in France's public finances may have been fueled by a worst-case scenario drawn up by ministry experts.
"Every year in January the budget department draws up 10 hypotheses on the outlook for the French economy and French finances, from the most catastrophic to the best-case scenario," he said.
"A rather catastrophic hypothesis has been published somewhere. The others have not been published," he said.
Both he and Arthuis said their confidence on the deficit was bolstered by the fact that France had made a very cautious official forecast on growth this year.
Growth would in fact be above the 2.3 percent forecast in the 1997 budget, Arthuis said.
Private economists said they saw no reason for a significant overshoot this year in France's total public deficit, which covers central government spending plus welfare and local authority accounts.
One official source, asked whether the overshoot could be as high as 50 billion francs, said this figure seemed "too high" but declined to say whether there would be a gap to be filled.

Last month, afternoon daily Le Monde said a worst-case scenario produced by ministry experts pointed to a public deficit of up to 3.8 percent of GDP this year. An overshoot of 0.8 percent would imply a shortfall of 67 billion francs.

Economists said the welfare system might show a gap slightly higher than the 35 billion francs forecast, though welfare system officials have said there is no evidence to suggest it would be significantly higher.
Tax receipts have also been reported by newspapers to be coming in lower than expected, although again economists said they could see no real evidence for this.
The government made a cautious forecast for VAT receipts in its 1997 budget.
The cost of servicing the national debt has been lower than expected, thanks to lower interest rates.
If the government were to need extra revenue to plug the budget gap, it could scrap some spending on top of the 10 billion francs in credit lines already frozen as a precaution against any overshoot.
The centre-right has also pledged to raise the CSG, a one-off tax on most income, to 5.4 percent from 3.4 percent from the summer in order to reduce payroll charges which weigh on the cost of labour.
It could decide against passing on all the revenues from the higher CSG into lower payroll charges, economists said.
-- Myra MacDonald Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5381
